onset

ON-set (stress on ON) · noun

Hear It

What It Means

The moment when something begins, especially something unwelcome that arrives on its own.

Doctors watched closely for the onset of symptoms.

Example

At the first onset of the hurricane's winds, the harbor crews had already tied down every boat.

Onset marks the moment the storm's arrival began - something sweeping in on its own schedule, which people can prepare for but cannot command.

How Strong Is It?

start → onset → outbreak

start vs. onset

start vs. onset: A start is milder than an onset: a start can begin anything at all, while an onset is the arrival of something that sweeps in on its own, often unwelcome.

outbreak vs. onset

outbreak vs. onset: An outbreak is stronger than an onset: an onset is the first moment something arrives, but an outbreak means it has burst out and is already spreading fast.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — on: upon, toward

root — set: to place, to begin

Put it together: Set on ('upon, toward') in front of set ('to place, to begin') and you get onset: the moment something 'sets upon' you. Long ago it named the start of an attack, which is why it still fits storms and illnesses that seem to charge in.

Use the root in a new word: sunset: We reached the beach just before sunset, when the daylight sets and slips below the water.

Root Check

Word Choice

Onset is kept for things that arrive on their own - the onset of winter, of a headache, of panic - usually things nobody wants. People do not schedule an onset; they brace for one. Its partner word in this unit is root: onset answers 'when did it begin?' while root answers 'what did it grow from?'.
